title: How do you write a CV that gets you a consulting interview?
description: What consulting recruiters look for on a CV, how to write achievement-led bullet points with numbers, and common mistakes to avoid.
hook: A CV that gets you a consulting interview proves three things fast: strong academics, real achievements with results, and leadership, ideally with something distinctive on top. Recruiters scan quickly, so every bullet should say what you did, how big it was and what changed because of it. A clean one-page layout and zero errors do the rest.
body:
What recruiters look for

  • Academic strength: grades, rankings, scholarships and test scores where they are relevant in your country.
  • Achievement: results you delivered, not responsibilities you held.
  • Leadership: times you led people, started something or took ownership without being asked.
  • Something distinctive: a sport at a high level, a business you started, a cause you built, a language you learned from scratch.

These map directly onto what interviews test later: problem solving, impact, leadership and drive. A CV that shows all four makes the screener's decision easy.

Write every bullet as a result

Give each bullet four parts, in whatever order reads most naturally: an action (a strong verb), the scope (how big), the outcome (what changed) and enough context to see why it mattered.

Weak: "Responsible for improving the sales reporting process."
Strong: "Rebuilt the weekly sales report for 12 stores, cutting preparation from six hours to one and letting managers spot stock-outs each morning."

The second tells the reader what you changed, at what scale and why it mattered. The same works for student roles:

Weak: "Responsible for the society's marketing."
Strong: "Redesigned the society's social media plan, growing event attendance from 40 to 150 in one term."

A worked example: getting the numbers right

Numbers make bullets credible, but only if they are correct and you can defend them in an interview. Three checks:

  1. Show the baseline. "Cut event costs by $3,000" means little alone. "Cut event costs by $3,000 (15%) on a $20,000 budget" is clear: $3,000 ÷ $20,000 = 15%.
  2. Know relative from absolute. If a sign-up rate rose from 10% to 13%, that is a 30% relative increase (3 ÷ 10) but only 3 percentage points. Write "raised sign-up rate from 10% to 13%" and let the reader see both.
  3. Annualise only if it is true. Saving five hours a week on a report is about 240 hours over a 48-week working year (5 × 48). Say "about 240 hours a year" only if the saving actually lasted.

Interviewers do ask, "How did you get that number?" A figure you cannot explain does more harm than no figure. This is the same habit that makes your case maths credible; our percentages tip is a quick refresher.

Not every achievement needs a revenue figure. An academic project can show analytical rigour, a volunteer role can show how you mobilised people, and a technical project can show a real user problem solved. What matters is a clear outcome.

Keep the layout clean

  • One page for students and early-career candidates.
  • A simple, consistent layout. No photos, graphics or colours unless that is the norm in your country.
  • Most recent first. Education at the top for students; experience first once you have a few years of work.
  • No unexplained acronyms. A recruiter outside your industry should understand every bullet.
  • Check every number, date and spelling. Mistakes suggest weak attention to detail, which consultants care about.

Cover letters

Where firms ask for one, keep it short and specific. Three parts work well: why consulting, why this firm (mention people you spoke to or work that interests you), and two or three pieces of evidence that you would be good at the job. Our tip on why consulting and why this firm shows how to make that motivation specific, and networking is how you get the details to put in it.

Common mistakes

  • Listing duties. "Responsible for..." describes the job, not you. Start with a verb and end with a result.
  • Vague intensifiers. "Significantly improved" says nothing. Quantify it or cut it.
  • Overclaiming. If a team of six delivered it, say what your part was.
  • One CV for every firm. Keep a master version, then reorder and trim for each application.
  • No outside reader. Ask someone unfamiliar with your work to explain each bullet back to you. If they cannot, rewrite it.

Practise now

1. Rewrite: "Helped with fundraising for a charity."

Show the answer

Ask what you did, how big it was and what changed. For example: "Organised a sponsored 10k for 35 runners, raising $8,400 for a local food bank, double the previous year's event." Use your real numbers; if you do not know them, find them before you write the bullet.

2. Your bullet says "Increased conversion by 25%". The rate went from 4% to 5%. Is the bullet accurate?

Show the answer

Yes, as a relative increase: (5 − 4) ÷ 4 = 25%. But it is only 1 percentage point, and an interviewer may push on it. Clearer: "Raised checkout conversion from 4% to 5% (a 25% relative increase) by simplifying the payment page."

3. You led a five-person student consulting project. Write one bullet.

Show the answer

"Led a five-person team advising a local café on pricing; recommended a new menu structure the owner adopted, raising average spend from $6.50 to $7.20 within two months." That is $0.70, about 11% more per customer. Leadership, scope and a defensible result in one line.

Where to go next

Once the CV is ready, see how the rest of recruiting works, and start preparing the stories behind your bullets with the fit interview guide.
